messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Mark Jensen was 61 when he came for treatment, a married American man who had spent years driving a city bus on early and late routes, preferring the predictability of the road to talking much about himself. What he finally described had happened decades earlier, during a period when he had been detained and tortured. Even in the first sessions, he did not tell it as one continuous story. He could give flashes with terrible precision and then stop at the edge of blankness. Some moments were fixed in him with unbearable clarity: the sound of approaching footsteps before a door opened, the instant he understood that other people near him were also in danger, the helpless certainty that he was about to be hurt again. Other stretches were missing altogether. He said it was as if his mind had kept a few frames in perfect focus and torn the rest out. What frightened him was not only what he remembered, but how little he could account for in between. He knew there had been more, and the gaps left him feeling unsteady, as if something essential had been lost but was still close enough to strike.

When he did remember, the emotional force was immediate. He did not speak of the torture as something far away that he could revisit at a distance. He said that when it came back, it brought the same terror. In session, he would stiffen, his breathing would change, and he would look toward the door before answering the next question. He spoke most painfully about the presence of others during that period and his conviction that he had failed them. He had come to believe, with the force of a moral verdict, that he should have done more to stop what happened and should have protected other people who were there. He did not present this as an abstract regret. To Mark, it was proof of something permanent about him. He was certain that a stronger man would have intervened, resisted, found some way to shield others. Because he had not, he called himself weak. “I failed,” he said in different forms again and again, as though any fuller account of the event would only confirm what he already knew.

Over the years, these experiences settled into his daily life in ways his family could see even when he said little. Nights were the worst. Daytime, with its routines and movement, gave him some structure, but darkness made him feel exposed. He found it harder to feel safe after sunset than at any other time. In bed he listened closely for sounds in and around the house, straining to detect whether someone might be entering. A settling floorboard, the rattle of a gate, a car door outside could bring a surge through his body so strong that he was instantly awake and braced. His wife had grown used to finding him up at the window or standing still in the hallway, listening. He knew the house was locked. He knew, in one sense, that he was at home. But what his body seemed to know was that danger announced itself in sounds before it arrived, and he could not stop himself from monitoring for it.

The same pattern followed him into work. Driving a bus meant long hours enclosed with strangers behind him and a constant stream of noise around him—passengers shifting, footsteps on the steps, the hydraulic hiss of the doors, sudden banging from the chassis or someone striking the side panel to get his attention. When a sharp sound caught him off guard, he felt the reaction before he could think: a jolt through his chest, tightening in his muscles, the sense of terror arriving all at once. He tried to keep his expression flat and his hands steady on the wheel, but he became more watchful on late routes, especially in the dark, checking mirrors repeatedly and listening to every movement near the front of the bus. He did not explain this much to coworkers. He told himself he was just being careful. Still, the strain accumulated. By the time he got home, he was already keyed up for the night ahead.

At home, his marriage had narrowed around these habits. His wife wanted to know what he needed, but Mark had little language for it besides saying he could not relax. He avoided fuller conversations about the torture because he dreaded what would happen if he tried to fill in the missing parts. At the same time, the parts he did remember punished him. He lived between blanks he could not tolerate and fragments he could not bear. What finally brought him to treatment was not a new event, but the growing sense that his life had become organized around fear and self-condemnation. After another night spent listening for an intruder and another workday shaken by sudden bodily surges at ordinary sounds, he told his wife he was tired of feeling as if the danger were still inside the house and inside him. He came in afraid that if he looked directly at the past, the terror would be exactly as overwhelming as it had been then. He also came in hoping, cautiously, that he might find some way to live at night, at home, and on his bus route without feeling that he had to stay on guard every minute.
